title: This is What a Knowledge Building Lesson Can Look Like 14, 2026
author: Science of Reading in the Classroom
source: Science of Reading in the Classroom (scienceofreadingclassroom.substack.com), September
summary: This piece uses a granular, minute-by-minute breakdown of a first-grade CKLA (Core Knowledge Language Arts) lesson, taught by teacher Stephane Bolton, to make an argument about the relationship between curriculum and instruction. The author's thesis is that adopting a knowledge-building curriculum is necessary but not sufficient — the curriculum supplies content, but teachers still make the moment-to-moment instructional decisions (when to interject, which response format to use, when to push for elaboration) that determine whether students actually build durable knowledge. The lesson walkthrough documents specific high-leverage routines: choral 'rapid retrieval practice' to force universal participation rather than calling on individuals, a multisyllabic-word-reading routine for previewing vocabulary instead of simply supplying definitions, and physical gestures tied to new vocabulary during a read-aloud to keep every student cognitively engaged. The piece explicitly pushes back on the common criticism that structured, knowledge-building curricula strip teachers of autonomy, arguing the opposite: the 'magic' in this lesson is entirely the teacher's skillful structuring choices layered on top of the curriculum's content foundation.
points: Shows a concrete technique for universal engagement: choral 'rapid retrieval practice' instead of calling on individual students, so everyone is retrieving content simultaneously.
Documents previewing new vocabulary through a multisyllabic-word-reading routine rather than simply handing students the words and definitions.
Pairs new vocabulary with physical gestures during a read-aloud so students are constantly, actively responding rather than passively listening.
Directly rebuts the 'knowledge-building curricula kill teacher autonomy' critique by showing how much moment-to-moment instructional judgment the lesson still requires.
quotes: Stephane doesn't call on students individually; she wants everyone thinking and retrieving previous content, so she expects students to respond chorally. Everyone is doing all of the work.
I love how Stephane expects her students to use a familiar multisyllabic word reading routine here, instead of just giving them the words.

Every time she encounters one of the new vocabulary words, she prompts the students to use the gesture they just learned. In other words, Stephane demands that ALL students respond to and think about the new material CONSTANTLY.

CKLA provides a strong foundation for this lesson, but the magic here is all Stephane. She decides how to structure the material: when to interject with questions, how to build in opportunities for retrieval practice or elaboration, when to use choral response vs. all-hands-up cold call, when to initiate a discussion.

One common critique of knowledge-building curriculum (and most structured curricula in general) is that they remove teacher autonomy. So, the next time you hear this critique, please share these instructional videos!
